newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Old S.Africa political foes merge to challenge ANC.
newsitem.headline: Old S.Africa political foes merge to challenge ANC.

text.p: A South African politician thrown out of President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress said on Wednesday he and a former rival were joining forces to challenge the ANC in 1999 elections.
Former parliamentarian Bantu Holomisa, expelled from the ANC on Mandela's orders last year, said he and white National Party dissident Roelf Meyer would launch a party on September 27.
The pair want to lobby for support across the race divide ahead of the 1999 polls, the second all-race election in South Africa's history.
"The party is going to participate in the 1999 election...We might surprise a few," Holomisa told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"One should not bite off more than one can chew. If we start out with a modest approach, I think we will get a start in 1999 and then we can build it from there," he said.

Meyer, co-architect of the post-apartheid constitution, fell out with former president F.W. de Klerk this year over his recommendation that the National Party should go into a new alliance capable of attracting significant black support.

Holomisa was deputy minister of environmental affairs and tourism after the 1994 all-race elections, but his relations with the ANC soured last year when he accused a fellow minister of accepting tainted money from a gambling tycoon.

The pair said in a statement after two days of talks this week that they had decided there was sufficient common ground to unite to promote a broad multi-party democracy as well as to pursue good governance and civil order.
"This will put our country on the road to becoming a winning nation," the joint statement said.
Mandela's ANC said in a statement on Wednesday that "talk of restructuring the political landscape in South Africa is nothing else but a chimera".

It added that a new political movement would not be able to deliver the social and economic reconstruction needed to correct apartheid inequalities. The party won 62 percent of the vote in the 1994 elections which swept Mandela to power.
